lead: Regularization adds a penalty to the regression coefficients. The penalty shrinks the coefficients, which reduces model variance and prevents over‑fitting. Ridge (L2) and Lasso (L1) are the two most common penalties and are used whenever many correlated features exist or when we want automatic feature selection.
prereq: You need: bias‑variance trade‑off from chapter 2.5 and linear regression from chapter 2.1.

blocks.text: In ordinary least squares we minimise the sum of squared errors (SSE), which is proportional to the mean‑squared error (MSE). When the training data are noisy, the fitted coefficients can become large and vary a lot with small changes in the data. Adding a penalty term to the loss forces the optimisation to prefer smaller coefficients. The penalty is controlled by a non‑negative number λ called the regularisation strength.

items: Large λ → strong shrinkage → high bias, low variance.
Small λ → little shrinkage → low bias, high variance.

blocks.text: Only a few universities teach Lasso in depth because the optimisation is not closed‑form. Both methods require the features to be on the same scale; otherwise the penalty would shrink some features more than others.
Ridge adds the sum of squared coefficients to the loss. The ridge loss is
Lridge = (1/n) Σ (y_i – ŷ_i)² + λ Σ w_j²
blocks.where: n is the number of training points; y_i is the true target; ŷ_i = w·x_i + b is the prediction; w_j are the feature coefficients; λ ≥ 0 controls the penalty.

blocks.text: Because the penalty is quadratic, the optimisation remains a convex quadratic problem with a closed‑form solution.

blocks.where: X is the n×p design matrix; y is the n‑vector of targets; I is the p×p identity matrix; n·λ I adds n·λ to each diagonal element of XᵀX. The intercept b is not regularised.

items: Standardise each column of X to mean 0 and variance 1.
Form the matrix XᵀX and add n·λ I.
Invert the resulting matrix and multiply by Xᵀy to obtain ŵ.
Do not regularise the intercept; keep it separate from the penalty.

blocks.text: Ridge never forces a coefficient exactly to zero, so all features stay in the model. It is useful when many features are correlated, as it distributes the weight among them.
Lasso adds the sum of absolute coefficients to the loss. The lasso loss is

blocks.where: All symbols are as defined for ridge; |w_j| is the absolute value of coefficient w_j.

blocks.text: The L1 penalty is not differentiable at zero, so there is no closed‑form solution. A common algorithm is coordinate descent.

items: Initialize all coefficient weights w_j to zero (the intercept b is handled separately and is not penalised).
For each coordinate j, compute the partial residual r_j = y – X_{‑j} w_{‑j}.
Update w_j using soft‑thresholding: w_j = S( (X_jᵀ r_j) / n , λ / n ), where S(z,γ) = sign(z)·max(|z|–γ,0).
Repeat until the change in all w_j is below a tolerance.

blocks.text: Because the soft‑thresholding can set w_j exactly to zero, lasso performs automatic feature selection. When many features are irrelevant, lasso yields a sparse model that is easier to interpret.

1. Split the data into training and validation sets. 2. Standardise the training features (subtract mean, divide by standard deviation) and apply the same transformation to validation data. 3. Use k‑fold cross‑validation on the training set to pick λ that gives the lowest validation MSE. 4. Retrain the chosen model on the full training set with the selected λ. 5. Evaluate on the held‑out test set.

items: Skipping standardisation leads to uneven shrinkage; the penalty will act more strongly on features with larger numeric range.
Very large λ makes all coefficients near zero – the model reduces to predicting the mean of y.
Very small λ recovers ordinary least squares.

blocks.text: The next chapter explains how to choose λ automatically using cross‑validation.

figure.caption: Coefficient magnitude versus λ for ridge (smooth decay) and lasso (sharp drop to zero).

spec.aria: Lines showing how ridge shrinks coefficients smoothly while lasso drives some to zero as λ increases.

examples.question: A used‑car price model uses two features: age (years) and mileage (thousands of km). The training data have not been standardised. For λ = 1, ridge regression gives coefficients w_age = 2.3 and w_mileage = 0.8. For λ = 0.5, lasso gives w_age = 2.1 and w_mileage = 0. Compute the predicted price for a car with age = 3 years and mileage = 40 000 km (i.e., mileage = 40). Assume the intercept term b = 5 (trained on raw features).
steps: Use the raw feature values directly as the model was trained on raw features.
Compute ridge prediction: ŷ_ridge = b + w_age·age + w_mileage·mileage = 5 + 2.3·3 + 0.8·40.
Compute lasso prediction: ŷ_lasso = 5 + 2.1·3 + 0·40 (mileage coefficient is zero).
examples.answer: Ridge predicts a price of 43.9 (in the raw scale). Lasso predicts 11.3.
examples.check:
age = 3
mileage = 40
b = 5
ridge_w_age = 2.3
ridge_w_mileage = 0.8
lasso_w_age = 2.1
lasso_w_mileage = 0
ridge_pred = b + ridge_w_age*age + ridge_w_mileage*mileage
lasso_pred = b + lasso_w_age*age + lasso_w_mileage*mileage
print(ridge_pred)
print(lasso_pred)

traps: Using raw features without standardisation makes λ shrink large‑scale features more than small‑scale ones.
Confusing the L1 penalty (∑|w|) with the L2 penalty (∑w²) leads to wrong formulae and wrong optimisation steps.
Setting λ = 0 in ridge or lasso does not automatically give the ordinary least‑squares solution if the implementation still adds a tiny regularisation term for numerical stability.
Assuming lasso always removes the same number of features regardless of λ; the number of zero coefficients depends on the data and λ value.
For ridge, forgetting to add λI to XᵀX (instead adding λ to every entry) produces a biased estimator.

quiz.q: Write the ridge loss function formula.
quiz.a: Lridge = (1/n) Σ (y_i – ŷ_i)² + λ Σ w_j².

quiz.q: Explain why standardising features is required before applying lasso.
quiz.a: Standardisation puts all features on the same scale, so the L1 penalty treats each coefficient equally. Without it, features with larger numeric range would be penalised more heavily, leading to biased shrinkage.

quiz.q: Given XᵀX = [[4,2],[2,3]] and λ = 1, compute the ridge coefficient vector ŵ assuming Xᵀy = [6,5] and no intercept.
For a single feature, the lasso soft‑thresholding update is w = S(z,γ). If z = 3.2 and γ = 1.5, compute the new w.
A dataset has two highly correlated features. Compare the effect of ridge versus lasso on the learned coefficients.
quiz.a: Ridge will distribute the weight between the correlated features, giving both non‑zero coefficients that are smaller than the OLS values. Lasso tends to pick one of the features and set the other’s coefficient to zero, leading to a sparse model.

quiz.q: What does the hyper‑parameter λ control in regularisation?
quiz.a: λ controls the strength of the penalty; larger λ means stronger shrinkage.

quiz.q: Why does lasso sometimes produce exactly zero coefficients while ridge never does?
quiz.a: The L1 penalty creates a kink at zero, and the optimisation uses soft‑thresholding which can set coefficients to exactly zero. The L2 penalty is smooth and quadratic, so the optimum is always at a point where the gradient is zero, which never forces a coefficient to be exactly zero.

quiz.q: You have trained a ridge model with λ = 0.2 and obtained coefficients [1.5, ‑0.8, 0.3]. If you double λ to 0.4, will any coefficient become zero? Explain.
quiz.a: No. Ridge shrinks coefficients smoothly; doubling λ reduces their magnitude but does not make any coefficient exactly zero.

beyond: Not for the exam. Regularisation is the basis of many modern techniques such as elastic‑net (a mix of L1 and L2), dropout in neural networks, and Bayesian priors on weights. In industry, ridge is used for large‑scale linear models like click‑through‑rate prediction, while lasso helps in gene‑selection problems in bio‑informatics. Recent research combines regularisation with deep learning to improve generalisation. To explore further, look for papers on "elastic‑net" and on "variational dropout".
